title: High Volume Edge
teaches: The High Volume Edge as we trade it: an up day on record volume in a lesser-known stock with a fresh story, its close (the HVC) marked with a ray and an AVWAP; the buy is day 2's dip under the HVC and trade back over it at market, the stop a few cents under the day-2 low, the first sell is a judgment, usually day 3 or later into a 3, 5 or 7 day push, with the rest trailed, and a close under the HVC is not a failure.

facts.quote: Our focus in the HVC setup is not just on any high volume but on the highest volume.
facts.claim: Duncan: the focus is not any high volume but the highest volume.

facts.quote: We ideally want to see the stock closing at 75% or higher of its daily range on the gap day. 50% is usually the lowest end DCR that I’ll trade.
facts.claim: Duncan wants a close at 75% or more of the day's range, 50% at the least.

facts.quote: The closing price of the gap-up day serves as our primary entry point.
facts.claim: Duncan buys the close of the gap-up day.

facts.quote: I typically set a hard stop-loss at 3-5% below the HVC.
facts.claim: Duncan's stop is 3% to 5% under the HVC.

facts.quote: An additional exit criterion is an end-of-day close below the HVC.
facts.claim: Duncan also exits on a close under the HVC.

facts.quote: This pattern occurs after a stock gaps up on huge volume due to earnings or another major news event.
facts.claim: Duncan: the pattern follows a gap on huge volume from earnings or major news.

facts.quote: In many cases the volume on earnings day might be the highest volume in the history of the stock or multi year high volume.
facts.claim: Bonde: the volume on a big earnings day is often the highest in the stock's history.

facts.quote: Earnings breakout on companies with significant analyst coverage do not do as well as the first kinds.
facts.claim: Bonde: earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well.

facts.quote: Stocks with no analyst coverage are typically smaller companies or companies which are out of favor.
facts.claim: Bonde: stocks with no analyst coverage are smaller or out of favor.

facts.quote: Because we track earnings daily most of the time we enter these kind of trades in pre market or at open.
facts.claim: Bonde enters these trades pre-market or at the open.

facts.quote: I rarely trade in extended hours but prefer to wait for the opening range highs
facts.claim: Kullamagi waits for the opening-range high on the gap day.

facts.quote: We can fix our anchor from meaningful market events, not just fixed time periods.
facts.claim: Shannon anchors a VWAP at a meaningful market event.

facts.quote: is anchored to a large price movement event.
facts.claim: Shannon's example anchors at a large price movement event.

facts.quote: Stop first (by default a few cents under the day's low or the prior day's low, F62); the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit the risk, skip the trade.
facts.claim: A3: stop first, a few cents under the day's low; the size comes from the stop; if the honest stop does not fit, skip.

facts.quote: The stop is the exit. It only moves up, never down or wider. The one exception is the gap rule (B20).
facts.claim: A4: the stop is the exit; it only moves up, never wider; the gap rule is the one exception.

facts.quote: Shares = account × risk % ÷ (entry − stop), rounded down, then capped: the size is the SMALLER of the risk-based size and the position cap
facts.claim: A5: shares are account times risk percent, divided by entry minus stop, rounded down, then capped.

facts.quote: Move the stop to breakeven at 2R to 5R, ideally. The first trim: the hard rule is a third at 3R; ideally anywhere from 3R to 6R, and in practice he mostly waits for 5R.
facts.claim: B19: breakeven between 2R and 5R; the hard rule for the first trim is a third at 3R.

facts.quote: A gap against the stop: the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide. The low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop.
facts.claim: B20: on a gap through the stop, the first 30-minute low is the new stop.

facts.quote: With a ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.
facts.claim: B20's ceiling: if the first 30 minutes take the loss past 2R, get out.

facts.quote: No new buys in the 3 days before an earnings report; hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R.
facts.claim: B22: no new buys in the 3 days before a report; hold through one only if up 5R.

facts.quote: The 200-day line: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long; shorts only below the 200-day, never above it unless it is a parabolic short.
facts.claim: B26: no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, except a parabolic long.

facts.quote: No chasing: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.
facts.claim: C28: never buy more than 4% above the buy point.

facts.quote: Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink (A5).
facts.claim: C28: chasing costs size, because the stop stays put and the distance grows.

facts.quote: Time stop: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money.
facts.claim: C33: a trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold.

facts.quote: Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
facts.claim: D41: a real stop order with the broker.

facts.quote: Never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume; illiquid stocks are not even watched.
facts.claim: D42: never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume.

facts.quote: After the first third at 3R: another third at 5R, then trail the last third; adjustable.
facts.claim: E51: another third at 5R, then trail the last third.

facts.quote: Entries are market orders.
facts.claim: E57: entries are market orders.

facts.quote: No new buys outside regular trading hours.
facts.claim: E58: no new buys outside regular hours.

facts.quote: The stop sits a few cents under the day's low, not exactly on it.
facts.claim: F62: the stop sits a few cents under the day's low.

facts.quote: If a stock opens above a trim level (3R, 5R), take that trim at the open.
facts.claim: F63: a trim level the day opens past is taken at the open.

facts.quote: The market reading as a guide (A10): Green, full risk per grade and up to 10 positions; Yellow, smaller and fewer; Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts.
facts.claim: F65: Green full risk; Yellow smaller and fewer; Orange only A+; Red mostly cash and shorts.

facts.quote: After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule.
facts.claim: B21: after a stop-out, buy again only on a new trigger, as a new trade.

facts.quote: A climax run on your own long (Bracco's parabolic burst): sell a big part into it, a judgment call.
facts.claim: C34: sell a big part into a climax run on your own long.

facts.quote: The full size at one price with one stop; no adding.
facts.claim: A5: full size at one price, one stop, no adding.

facts.quote: No setup, no trade: never force a trade to have something on; cash is a position.
facts.claim: D44: no setup, no trade; cash is a position.

facts.quote: A lesser-known stock, often neglected or beaten down, with no prior trend required. A fresh story arrives all at once.
facts.claim: The context: a lesser-known, often neglected stock; a fresh story arrives all at once.

facts.quote: Its close is the HVC, a level marked with a ray and an AVWAP for months.
facts.claim: The record day's close is the HVC, marked with a ray and an AVWAP.

facts.quote: RED TO GREEN on day 2: the session after the HVE opens at or under the HVC, trades under it, then trades back over it; a market order a cent over the HVC.
facts.claim: The trigger: day 2 opens at or under the HVC, trades under, then back over; buy at market a cent over.

facts.quote: A few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim. Never the HVC itself, and never the HVE low on a day-2 entry.
facts.claim: The stop: a few cents under the day-2 low; never the HVC, never the HVE low.

facts.quote: Day 2 reclaims the HVC and closes back under the fill, or the stock slices back under the HVE low within weeks and the level turns into overhead.
facts.claim: The failure mode: a close back under the fill, or a slide under the HVE low that turns the level into overhead.

facts.quote: The trade, not the HVE day, is above the 200-day SMA at the moment of entry.
facts.claim: The trade, not the HVE day, must be above the 200-day at entry.

facts.quote: A fresh story: a contract, a trial result, a partnership, a government stake, an IPO-year re-rating, or earnings so big the volume is extreme. Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.
facts.claim: A fresh story; earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.

facts.quote: An up close: the HVE day closes over the prior close. Long only.
facts.claim: The HVE day closes up; long only.

facts.claim: Never the monthly options expiry or a month's last session.

facts.quote: Not a climax: not after a run of 60% or more in the prior 60 sessions, and not on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst.
facts.claim: Not after a 60% run in 60 sessions, not on day 3 to 5 of a straight-up burst.

facts.claim: Mark a ray at the HVC and an AVWAP from the HVE day; later setups form there.

facts.claim: The taught trigger is day 2, not the HVE close or a later day.

facts.claim: Day 2 must open at or under the HVC and trade under it.

facts.quote: Red to green through the HVC: the moment day 2 trades back over the HVE close, buy with a market order a cent over the HVC.
facts.claim: Buy at market a cent over the HVC the moment day 2 trades back over it.

facts.quote: No buy more than 4% over the HVC; the HVC is the buy point.

questions.q: On a High Volume Edge, what is the HVC?
choices: The record day's close
The record day's high
The record day's low
The next session's open
questions.why: The record day's close. The HVC is the closing price of the record-volume up day. You mark it with a ray and an AVWAP and keep both on the chart for months. It is not the day's high or low. It is not day 2's open either. Day 2's open is only where the trigger starts.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is the record day's close. That is the line.

wrong.The record day's high: The high is not the level. The card marks the close.
wrong.The record day's low: The low matters later, for the level. The HVC itself is the close.
wrong.The next session's open: Day 2's open is where the trigger starts. The level is the record day's close.

questions.simple: The HVC is the close of the record volume day. We mark that price and watch it for months.

reasons: three card facts, a settled definition

questions.q: A High Volume Edge is an up day: the record day closes over the prior close.
questions.why: True. The record day closes over the prior close, and we trade the setup long only. A record-volume day that closed down is never an HVE. Shorting a down-close record day is a named mistake.
questions.lesson_line: Record volume and an up close. Both, or it is not an HVE.
questions.simple: True. An HVE day must close above the day before, and we only trade it long.

reasons: settled up-close and long-only rules

questions.q: When is the taught High Volume Edge buy?
choices: Day 2, the next session
At the record close
At the record open
Day 3, if day 2 holds
questions.why: Day 2, the next session. The taught trigger is the one session after the record day. Day 2 dips under the record day's close and reclaims it, and that is the buy. It is not the record day's close, and not a later day. Duncan buys the gap-up day's close, and the Episodic Pivot is bought on the gap day itself. The High Volume Edge waits a session.
questions.lesson_line: The record day marks the level. Day 2 gives the trade.

wrong.At the record close: The close is the level, not the buy. The taught trigger waits for day 2.
wrong.At the record open: That is the Episodic Pivot's day: bought on the gap day itself. The HVE waits a session.
wrong.Day 3, if day 2 holds: Not a later day. The taught trigger is the one session after the record day.

questions.simple: Buy on day 2, the session after the record day, not on the record day itself.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's day-2 trigger and the held D-005 (whether a close entry is taught at all)

questions.q: On the day-2 entry the stop goes a few cents under the day-2 low.
questions.why: True. The stop sits a few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim, and not exactly on it. Stop first: the size comes from the stop. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, you skip the trade.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first: a few cents under the day-2 low.
questions.simple: True. The stop goes a few cents under the day-2 low, so it never sits exactly on that low.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62, settled)

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: Draw a ray at the HVC, then add the ___ from the record day.
questions.why: An anchored VWAP. We mark a ray at the HVC and an AVWAP anchored on the record day. We keep both on the chart for months. Later setups form at that level. Shannon anchors a VWAP at a meaningful market event, not just at fixed time periods.
questions.lesson_line: Two marks on the chart: a ray at the close, an AVWAP from the day.
questions.simple: Draw an anchored VWAP that starts on the record day, next to the ray at the close.

reasons: settled chart marks, two facts

questions.q: A record-volume day on the monthly options expiry, the third Friday, can count as a High Volume Edge.
questions.why: False. The monthly options expiry, the third Friday, never counts as a High Volume Edge day. The volume on that day is not demand, so check the calendar before you trust the volume. A record day on any other date still has to pass the rest of the checks.
questions.lesson_line: Check the calendar before the volume. Expiry day volume is not demand.
questions.simple: False. Volume on the monthly options expiry is not real demand, so that day never counts.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (the card's excluded-days line)
+2 rests on the card and the held D-092 (more excluded days may be added)

questions.q: Day 2 opens under the HVC and trades lower. What is the trigger?
choices: A trade back over the HVC
A close back over the HVC
A trade over the HVE day's high
A bounce off the day-2 low
questions.answer: A trade back over the HVC
questions.why: A trade back over the HVC. Day 2 opens at or under the HVC and trades under it. The moment it trades back over, that red to green move is the trigger. Buy with a market order a cent over the HVC. You do not wait for a close, and the line is the HVC, not the record day's high.
questions.lesson_line: Under, then back over the HVC. That is the trigger.

wrong.A close back over the HVC: The trigger is intraday. Entries are market orders the moment it trades back over.
wrong.A trade over the HVE day's high: The line is the HVC, the record day's close, not its high.
wrong.A bounce off the day-2 low: The day-2 low is where the stop goes, a few cents under it. The trigger is the trade back over the HVC.

questions.simple: Buy the moment price trades back over the record day's close after dipping under it. You do not wait for a close.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E57, entries are market orders) and the card's trigger

questions.q: The HVC itself is a good place for the High Volume Edge stop.
questions.why: False. The HVC is never the stop. Price trades under it in 98% of cases within 60 sessions, so a stop there is very likely to be hit. The stop goes a few cents under the day-2 low instead.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is a level to watch, not a stop to sit on.
questions.simple: False. The HVC is never the stop, because price trades back under it in almost every case within 60 sessions.

reasons: +2 a statistic (98% within 60 sessions) from the card's own research that can change when it is re-run
+2 rests on the card's stop rule and the owner's ruling that going under the HVC is fine

questions.q: Which story fits a High Volume Edge?
choices: A trial win in a quiet stock
An ordinary earnings beat
A slow drift up on rising volume
A mega-cap's busy earnings day
questions.answer: A trial win in a quiet stock
questions.why: A trial win in a quiet stock. A fresh story arrives all at once, such as a contract, a trial result or a partnership, in a lesser-known stock. Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.
questions.lesson_line: Ask what changed. A new story makes an HVE; a routine beat does not.

wrong.An ordinary earnings beat: Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, not an HVE.
wrong.A slow drift up on rising volume: A fresh story arrives all at once. A slow drift is not a record day on new news.
wrong.A mega-cap's busy earnings day: Not a mega-cap. A big day in a mega-cap is an HVC, not an HVE.

questions.simple: A fresh story in a quiet stock fits. A routine beat, a slow drift or a mega-cap's big day does not.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's fresh-story line (c07, c01) and the mega-cap mistake (c36)

questions.q: A High Volume Edge needs no prior advance before the record day.
questions.why: True. No prior advance is required. The HVE is often the first day of a new story, and no prior trend is needed. The card sets a ceiling instead. A run of 60% or more in the prior 60 sessions makes the day a climax, not a start.
questions.lesson_line: No run-up needed. The record day is often the start.
questions.simple: True. No earlier run-up is needed, because the record day is often the first day of a new story.

reasons: +2 the card lists no_prior_trend and the 60% climax line (not_climax) as proposed, not settled

questions.q: Day 2 opens over the HVC and stays over it all session. Is that our trigger?
choices: No; it must dip under first
Yes; it is strong, holding above
Yes; buy the open over the HVC
No; it needs a close over it
questions.answer: No; it must dip under first
questions.why: No. Day 2 must open at or under the HVC and trade under it before the reclaim. A day 2 that opens over the HVC and never trades under it is not this trigger. It may become a later entry, with its own trigger and stop. Strength alone is not the trigger, and the open over the HVC is not a buy.
questions.lesson_line: No dip under the HVC, no day-2 trade.

wrong.Yes; it is strong, holding above: Strength is not the trigger here. The trigger is under, then back over.
wrong.Yes; buy the open over the HVC: Buying the open over the HVC is not our trade. Day 2 has to dip and reclaim.
wrong.No; it needs a close over it: No close is needed. The trigger is a dip under, then an intraday trade back over.

questions.simple: No. Day 2 has to dip under the HVC and then trade back over it, and this one never dipped.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed day-2 dip rule

questions.q: On big enough news we buy a High Volume Edge pre-market, as Bonde does.
questions.why: False. No buys outside regular trading hours. Bonde enters these trades pre-market or at the open, and we do not. The news can arrive before the open, but our buy waits for the session after the record day.
questions.lesson_line: Regular hours only. The news can wait for the bell.
questions.simple: False. We buy only in regular trading hours, so no pre-market buys, even though Bonde buys pre-market.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (E58, no buys outside regular hours)

questions.q: Tap the number that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: Never buy a High Volume Edge more than ___ over the HVC.
questions.why: 4%. No buy more than 4% over the HVC; the HVC is the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays under the buy point, so the distance grows and the shares shrink. A market buy a cent over the HVC sits well inside the limit.
questions.lesson_line: The HVC is the buy point. Past 4% over it, you are chasing.
questions.simple: 4%. We never buy more than 4% over the HVC, because past that you are chasing.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% chase limit)

questions.q: When price closes under the HVC, the level is broken and comes off the chart.
questions.why: False. Trading or closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level. Do not erase it.
questions.lesson_line: Under the HVC is normal. Keep the line on the chart.

questions.q: Which name fits a High Volume Edge best?
choices: A thinly owned small company
A mega-cap everyone owns
A small cap widely covered
A hot leader up a lot
questions.why: A thinly owned small company. The card wants a lesser-known stock, often neglected or beaten down, where a fresh story arrives all at once. It does not want a mega-cap. Bonde adds that earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well. Stocks with no analyst coverage are typically smaller or out of favor.
questions.lesson_line: The less known the name, the bigger the new story.

wrong.A mega-cap everyone owns: Not a mega-cap. The card wants a lesser-known stock and rules the mega-cap out.
wrong.A small cap widely covered: Bonde: earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well.
wrong.A hot leader up a lot: A big run first can turn the day into a climax. The card wants a quiet, lesser-known name.

questions.simple: The card wants a lesser-known, neglected company, where a fresh story arrives all at once.

reasons: the lesser-known cue is a proposed card line

questions.q: You hold a High Volume Edge that is working. A pullback to the HVC is no reason to add shares.
questions.why: True. Full size goes in at one price with one stop, with no adding. A pullback to the HVC does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: One price, one stop, one size. No adds.
questions.simple: True. Full size goes in at one price with one stop, so you do not add on a pullback.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, no adding)

questions.q: What is it?
questions.story: A stock trades the most shares in its history. It finishes the day 15% under the prior close.
choices: Not an HVE; it closed down
An HVE short
An HVE; record volume is enough
Not yet; day 2 decides it
questions.answer: Not an HVE; it closed down
questions.why: Not an HVE. The day must close over the prior close, and a record-volume day that closed down is never an HVE. Here it closed down 15%. We trade this setup long only, so shorting it is a named mistake. A later day-2 reclaim cannot change how the record day closed.
questions.lesson_line: Check the colour of the record bar first.

wrong.An HVE short: We trade the HVE long only. Shorting a down-close record day is a named mistake.
wrong.An HVE; record volume is enough: Record volume is half of it. The day must close up.
wrong.Not yet; day 2 decides it: The down close already rules the record day out. A later reclaim cannot make it an HVE.

questions.simple: It is not an HVE, because the day closed down. Record volume alone is not enough, and we do not short it.

reasons: +2 the held D-091 (what a down-close record day is called) sits next to this; the key uses only the settled up-close line

questions.q: Our rule bars new buys in a window before an earnings report. How long is the window?
choices: 1 day
3 days
5 days
10 days
questions.why: 3 days. We take no new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report. An earnings HVE falls just after a report, so this binds the later entries.
questions.lesson_line: Three days before a report, no new buys.

wrong.1 day: Too short. The window is 3 days.
wrong.5 days: Too long. The window is 3 days.
wrong.10 days: That is the time stop, 10 trading days. The report window is 3 days.

questions.simple: 3 days. We take no new buy in the 3 days before an earnings report.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B22); the rulebook says 3 days and the card says 3 sessions

questions.q: Bought at 56.28 with the stop at 55.53. Where is 3R?
questions.why: $58.53. One R is the fill minus the stop, 56.28 minus 55.53. Add three of those to the 56.28 fill. 3R is a measuring mark, so know the price before the buy.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is a measuring mark. Know its price before the buy.
questions.simple: 58.53. The risk is the buy minus the stop, and 3R is the buy plus three times that risk.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19, a third at 3R)
+1 fixed before (the fill was corrected)

wrong.$57.78: Added three R to the stop, not the fill.
wrong.$59.28: Counted four R, one too many.

questions.q: On a High Volume Edge winner the stop stays at the day-2 low until the last third is sold.
questions.why: False. The stop moves up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default. A stop only moves up, never down or wider. So the stop should be above the day-2 low well before the last third is sold.
questions.lesson_line: At the first trim, the stop goes to breakeven.
questions.simple: False. The stop moves up to breakeven between 2R and 5R, at the first trim by default, not at the last third.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B19); the card's failure notes put the move at 2R while its management line says the first trim

questions.q: The market reading is Orange. Which High Volume Edge trades may you take?
choices: Only A+ setups
Full risk per grade
Any grade, but smaller size
Mostly cash and shorts
questions.why: Only A+ setups. The market reading is a guide to how much you play. In an Orange market we take only A+ setups.
questions.lesson_line: The market sets how much you play.

wrong.Full risk per grade: Orange is not full risk. It is A+ only.
wrong.Mostly cash and shorts: Orange still allows A+ setups. It is not mostly cash.
wrong.Any grade, but smaller size: Orange limits the grade. It is A+ only.

questions.simple: In an Orange market you take only A+ setups.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A10 and F65, the market reading as a guide)

questions.q: Buy or pass?
questions.story: The HVC is 20.00. Day 2 dipped to 19.40 and reclaimed it while you were away. It now trades 21.10.
choices: Pass; it is 5.5% over the HVC
Buy; it is only 3% over the HVC
Buy half; it is close enough
Buy with the stop at 20.00
questions.answer: Pass; it is 5.5% over the HVC
questions.why: Pass. 21.10 is 5.5% over the 20.00 HVC, past the 4% chase limit. You never buy more than 4% above the buy point. Chasing costs size, not risk: the stop stays put, the distance grows and the shares shrink. Missing the reclaim means letting this one go, or waiting for a later setup at the level.
questions.lesson_line: Missed the reclaim: let it go, or wait for a later setup at the level.

wrong.Buy half; it is close enough: Half size does not cure a chase. Past 4% is a pass.
wrong.Buy with the stop at 20.00: A different stop does not cure a chase. Past 4% over the HVC is a pass.
wrong.Buy; it is only 3% over the HVC: It is 5.5% over the 20.00 HVC, not 3%. Past the 4% limit is a pass.

questions.simple: Pass. At 21.10 the stock is more than 4% over the HVC, so buying now is chasing.

deeper.trap: The trap is a fix that sounds careful. A half-size buy or a stop moved to 20.00 does not cure a chase, because the rule is about where you buy. Missing the reclaim means letting this one go. If price pulls back to the level, a later setup there has its own trigger and stop.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C28, the 4% chase limit)
+1 fixed before (a wrong note was edited)

questions.q: Ten trading days after your day-2 buy the trade sits at 0.6R. Our rule?
choices: Sell it and free the money
Hold; the level is still there
Sell half and hold the rest
Move the stop to breakeven
questions.answer: Sell it and free the money
questions.why: Sell it. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, freeing the money. At 0.6R it is still under 1R. The level staying on the chart does not change this. Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, so it is not due yet.
questions.lesson_line: Ten days and under 1R: let it go.

wrong.Hold; the level is still there: The level stays on the chart. The trade still goes after 10 days under 1R.
wrong.Move the stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R. At 0.6R after 10 days the time stop applies.
wrong.Sell half and hold the rest: The rule sells the trade, not half of it. A trade under 1R after 10 days is sold.

questions.simple: Sell. A trade still under 1R after 10 trading days is sold, so the money is free for a better use.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (C33, the time stop)

questions.q: Tap the words that fit the blank.
questions.sentence: Your protective exit on the day-2 buy is a real ___ with the broker.
questions.why: A stop order. Every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. It only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: The stop lives with the broker, not in your head.
questions.simple: A stop order. It is a real order with the broker, not a stop you keep in your head.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, a real stop order)

questions.q: Fill 58.13. The day-2 low is 57.56. The stop sits two cents under it. How far below the fill, in percent to one decimal?
questions.why: 1.0%. The stop is two cents under the day-2 low: 57.56 minus 0.02. The fill minus that stop, over the fill, 58.13, is 1.0%. Stop first, then the distance, then the size.
questions.lesson_line: Stop first, distance second, size last.
questions.simple: About 1.0%. The stop is two cents under the day-2 low of 57.56, a little under the 58.13 fill.

deeper.trap: The tight stop is the design, not a flaw. In the failed trades the day-2 stops were 1.7% to 3.5% wide, and the first sessions decide the trade. When NAVN's honest stop was 7.5% wide, the answer was never to pull the stop in. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, you skip the trade.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A3 and F62)
+1 fixed before (the fill was corrected)

wrong.0.6%: Read the dollar gap as a percent.
wrong.10.1%: Slipped the decimal one place to the right.
wrong.99.0%: Divided the stop by the fill and skipped the subtraction.

questions.q: The stock averages 3,000,000 shares a day after the event. By our volume rule, the most shares you may own?
questions.why: 30,000 shares. We never own more than 1% of a stock's average daily volume, measured on the post-event average. 1% of 3,000,000 shares is 30,000. Illiquid stocks are not even watched.
questions.lesson_line: Own no more than 1% of a day's volume.
questions.simple: 30,000 shares. You never own more than 1% of the average daily volume, and 1% of 3,000,000 is 30,000.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D42, 1% of average daily volume)

choices: 30,000 shares
300,000 shares
60,000 shares
3,000,000 shares

wrong.300,000 shares: Took ten percent of the volume, not one percent.
wrong.3,000,000 shares: Used the whole average daily volume as the limit.

questions.q: Bought at 84.90, stop 83.38. The stock trades 92.50. How many R is that?
questions.why: 5.0R. R is the buy minus the stop, 84.90 minus 83.38. The gain is 92.50 minus 84.90. Divide the gain by R to get 5.0R. About 5 to 10R is often a good place to sell. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed level.
questions.lesson_line: Count the gain in R. Around 5R to 10R is often where we sell.
questions.simple: 5.0R. The gain is five times the risk, and 5R is around where we often start selling.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook and the held D-024 (the trail line is not set)
+1 fixed before (the fill was corrected)

wrong.0.2R: Flipped it: divided the risk by the gain.
wrong.6.0R: Measured the gain from the stop, not from the buy.
wrong.7.6R: Used the dollar gain and never divided by the risk.

questions.q: Before the record day the stock traded 2,500,000 shares a day at 12.00. How many dollars a day is that?
questions.why: $30,000,000 a day: 2,500,000 shares times 12.00. The card calls a stock lesser-known when its dollar volume before the event is under about $100 million a day. It must not be a mega-cap. At $30 million this name is well under that cue.
questions.lesson_line: Read the dollar volume before the day. Small means lesser-known.
questions.simple: $30 million a day. That is small, well under the card's cue of about $100 million, so the name counts as lesser-known.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the card's proposed $100 million cue

questions.q: HVE or something else?
questions.story: A widely owned stock gaps up on earnings and closes 28.1% higher. Volume tops the past year but barely beats the old high. Day 2 dips and reclaims the close.
choices: A PEG; big but ordinary volume
An HVE; the day-2 reclaim triggers
An HVE; the earnings gap is big
An Episodic Pivot; it gapped on news
questions.answer: A PEG; big but ordinary volume
questions.why: A PEG, a Power Earnings Gap, not an HVE. An earnings gap on big but ordinary volume in a well-owned name is a PEG. Rank the volume, not the gap. An earnings gap is an HVE only when the volume is extreme. ROKU looked like this: +28.1%, a one-year record, a day-2 dip and reclaim. Taken as an HVE it was stopped at 0.0R.
questions.lesson_line: Rank the volume, not the gap.

wrong.An HVE; the day-2 reclaim triggers: The trigger is fine. The record day is not an HVE: the volume is ordinary for this name.
wrong.An HVE; the earnings gap is big: The gap does not make it. Rank the volume, not the gap.
wrong.An Episodic Pivot; it gapped on news: An EP is bought on the gap day itself over the opening-range high. By day 2 that entry has passed.

questions.simple: A PEG, a Power Earnings Gap. A big earnings gap on ordinary volume in a widely owned stock is not an HVE.

deeper.trap: Record and big are not the same. ROKU passed every other test: +28.1%, a close at 0.99 of the range, a day-2 dip of 2.8% and a reclaim. But its volume was only a one-year record in a name that traded $773M a day, so it was a PEG.

reasons: ties to held decision D-089 (record volume); the key holds under every option

questions.q: What is the trade on day 2?
questions.story: A stock rises 29% on the most shares it has ever traded and closes near the high. Day 2 opens 2.1% over that close. Its low stays 1.7% above it.
choices: No trigger; it never dipped under
Buy the open; strength is the tell
Buy, stop under the HVC
Short it; the gap will fill
questions.answer: No trigger; it never dipped under
questions.why: No trigger. Day 2 opened 2.1% over the HVC and its low stayed 1.7% over it. A valid HVE day, no day-2 trade.
questions.lesson_line: A strong day 2 is not our trigger. Wait for a later setup at the level.

wrong.Buy the open; strength is the tell: Our trigger needs a dip under the HVC first. This one never dipped.
wrong.Buy, stop under the HVC: The HVC is never the stop, and there was no trigger.
wrong.Short it; the gap will fill: We trade the HVE long only.

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The HVC is 13.11. Day 2 opens at 12.80 and trades lower. Midday it trades back up to 13.12.
choices: Buy at market, a cent over
Wait for a close over 13.11
Place a limit at 12.80
Wait for a new high
questions.answer: Buy at market, a cent over
questions.why: Buy at market, a cent over the HVC. Red to green through the HVC is the trigger, and entries are market orders.
questions.lesson_line: Set the alert at the HVC. When it trades back over, buy at market.

wrong.Wait for a close over 13.11: The trigger is intraday, the moment it trades back over.
wrong.Place a limit at 12.80: Entries are market orders, and 12.80 is under the trigger.
wrong.Wait for a new high: The line is the HVC. A new high comes later and past the chase limit.

questions.q: Start or climax?
questions.story: The stock is on its fourth straight up day, each one gapping higher. Today it trades record volume and closes up 25%.
choices: A climax; not our HVE
A start; plan day 2
A start; buy close
A climax; play day 2
questions.why: A climax. The card rules out a record day on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst. It also rules out a day after a run of 60% or more in the prior 60 sessions. This is the fourth straight up day, each gapping higher, so it is a climax and not a start. There is no day 2 to plan.
questions.lesson_line: A record at the start is a beginning. A record at the end of a burst is a climax.

wrong.A start; plan day 2: Not on the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst. This is the fourth.
wrong.A start; buy close: The close is the level, not the buy, and this day is a climax.
wrong.A climax; play day 2: A climax day is no HVE, so there is no day 2 to plan.

questions.simple: A record on the fourth straight up day is a climax, so it is not our setup.

deeper.trap: A climax has two tests, and either one rules the day out. One is a run of 60% or more in the prior 60 sessions. The other is the third to fifth day of a straight-up burst. A stock can fail the burst test with no 60% run behind it.

reasons: one cited fact only (the climax line on the card)

questions.q: If a gap through your stop takes the loss past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you get out.
questions.why: True. On a gap through the stop, the first 30 minutes of the gap-down day decide, and 2R is the ceiling. Past 2R, get out. HVE names gap often, so this rule is not rare.
questions.lesson_line: Past 2R in the first 30 minutes after a gap: you are out.
questions.simple: True. If a gap takes the loss past 2R in the first 30 minutes, you are out.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: You bought your High Volume Edge long yesterday, and it closed at 2.7R. This morning, day 2, it gaps open at 3.5R.
choices: Hold it all; day 3 is the earliest
Sell a third at the open, 3.5R
Sell the whole position at the open
Sell half at the open, bank the gap
questions.answer: Hold it all; day 3 is the earliest
questions.why: Hold it all. We very rarely sell on day 1 of a buy and usually wait until day 3 at the earliest. The first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. A gap to 3.5R on day 2 does not change that.
questions.lesson_line: A gap through 3R on day 2 is not a sell. Day 3 at the earliest.

wrong.Sell a third at the open, 3.5R: A fixed third at 3R is not our rule. The first sell is a judgment, usually from day 3 on.
wrong.Sell the whole position at the open: Selling everything this early misses the multi-week trend. We sell part and trail the rest.
wrong.Sell half at the open, bank the gap: Half is still an early fixed sell. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.

questions.simple: Hold. The first sell is a judgment, and we usually wait until day 3 at the earliest, even after a gap to 3.5R.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F63 trim at the open)

questions.q: The stock sat under its 200-day for months, until the record day. Day 2's fill is above the line. Does it pass the 200-day rule?
choices: Yes; the rule reads it at entry
No; it sat under the line before
Yes; but only after a close over it
No; only a parabolic long can
questions.answer: Yes; the rule reads it at entry
questions.why: Yes. The trade, not the HVE day, must be above the 200-day at the moment of entry. Our rule is no longs below the 200-day simple moving average, unless it is a parabolic long. Here the fill is above it, so where the stock sat before the record day does not matter.
questions.lesson_line: Judge the 200-day at the fill, not on the record day.

wrong.No; only a parabolic long can: That exception covers a long below the 200-day. This fill is above it, so the plain rule is met.
wrong.No; it sat under the line before: Where it sat before does not decide. The 200-day is read at entry.
wrong.Yes; but only after a close over it: No close is needed. The 200-day is read at the moment of entry.

questions.simple: Yes. The rule checks the 200-day line at your entry, not on the days before.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B26 200-day line)

questions.q: Which record-volume up day never counts as a High Volume Edge?
choices: The last session of the month
The first session of a month
A day on a trial result
A day in a beaten-down stock
questions.answer: The last session of the month
questions.why: The last session of the month. The card bars it, because the volume on that day is not demand. A trial result is the kind of fresh story the card wants, and a beaten-down stock can qualify because no prior advance is required.
questions.lesson_line: Month-end volume is not demand.

wrong.The first session of a month: The card does not bar the first session.
wrong.A day on a trial result: A trial result is a fresh story, the kind the card wants.
wrong.A day in a beaten-down stock: Beaten-down is often where it starts. No prior trend is needed.

questions.simple: The last session of the month never counts, because that volume is not real demand. The first session does not.

reasons: +3 the key rests on one cited fact (the excluded-days line)
+2 rests on the card and the held D-092 (more excluded days may be added)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: Six sessions after your day-2 buy the stock closes under the HVC. Your stop under the day-2 low has not traded.
choices: Hold; the stop is the exit
Hold; out on second close
Sell now; the level broke
Widen the stop for room
questions.answer: Hold; the stop is the exit
questions.why: Hold. Closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level. Do not erase it, and do not sell for that reason alone. The stop is the exit, and yours under the day-2 low has not traded. Price trades under the HVC in 98% of cases within 60 sessions.
questions.lesson_line: Under the HVC is normal. The stop, not the line, ends the trade.

wrong.Hold; out on second close: The stop is the exit. Trading or closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level.
wrong.Sell now; the level broke: A close under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level. The stop is the exit.
wrong.Widen the stop for room: The stop only moves up, never wider.

questions.simple: Hold. A close under the HVC does not end the trade, only the stop does.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit)

questions.q: What is the HVC now?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 55.46 with a stop at 53.73. It traded two sessions later, a planned loss. Weeks on, the stock closes under the record day's low.
choices: A ceiling above price
Support; buy again
Broken; erase it
The new stop level
questions.why: A ceiling above price. A close under the HVE day's low ends the level as support. After that the HVC is overhead, not a floor. Keep it on the chart anyway. QGEN slid to 38.80, under its 46.07 HVE low, and the level turned into overhead.
questions.lesson_line: Under the record day's low, the HVC turns from floor to ceiling.

wrong.Support; buy again: Under the record day's low it is no longer support. A new buy needs a new trigger.
wrong.Broken; erase it: Do not erase it. The level stays on the chart, and it now sits overhead.
wrong.The new stop level: You are out already. The line now sits overhead.

questions.simple: After a close under the record day's low, the HVC is a ceiling above price, not a floor.

reasons: the level rule is proposed on the card

questions.q: Was the stop a mistake?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 80.07, stop 77.24. The next session takes your stop, and within three sessions the low is 71.08. Weeks later it runs to 88.84.
choices: No; the stop is the exit
Yes; it needed a wider stop
Yes; you should have held
No; but you sized it too big
questions.answer: No; the stop is the exit
questions.why: No. The stop is the exit, and you followed the plan. A stop that trades before a run is the cost of a tight stop, not a reason to widen it. The stop only moves up, never wider. The size came from the stop, so the loss was the planned risk.
questions.lesson_line: A loss taken at plan is the system working.

wrong.Yes; it needed a wider stop: Room is not the answer. A stop that trades before a run is the cost of a tight stop; the stop only moves up.
wrong.Yes; you should have held: Holding past the stop is not in the plan. The stop is the exit.
wrong.No; but you sized it too big: The size came from the stop, so the loss was the planned risk. Nothing went wrong.

questions.simple: No. The stop is the exit, so a planned loss is the plan working, even if the stock runs later.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A4, the stop is the exit; B21)
+1 fixed before (the story was corrected)

questions.q: Buy it back?
questions.story: Stopped out the day after your day-2 buy, you watch the stock grind back up, well over the HVC.
choices: Only on a new trigger
Yes; it is back over the HVC
Only with a smaller size
Never; the stock failed you
questions.why: Only on a new trigger. After a stop-out, buy again only if the setup triggers again, as a new trade with its own stop and every rule. Each later entry at the level has its own trigger and stop. Being back over the HVC is not a trigger.
questions.lesson_line: Stopped out: the next trade needs its own trigger.

wrong.Yes; it is back over the HVC: Being over the HVC is not a trigger. The new trade needs its own setup.
wrong.Never; the stock failed you: Not never. A new trigger is a new trade with its own stop.
wrong.Only with a smaller size: Size is not the test. A re-entry is a new trade with its own trigger and stop.

questions.simple: Only if the setup triggers again. A stop-out ends that trade, and a new buy is a new trade with its own stop.

deeper.counter: The pull to buy back is strongest when the stock runs without you. SE was stopped the next session, then ran to 88.84 with no new day-2 trigger, then collapsed to 56.05. No new trigger meant no new trade, and the run was not a reason to chase it.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (B21, a new trade after a stop-out)
+1 fixed before (a wrong note was edited)

questions.q: Your High Volume Edge long runs four straight days, each gapping higher on rising volume. Our rule?
choices: Sell a big part into it
Sell a small part and trail
Add more on the next gap
Move the stop to the HVC
questions.answer: Sell a big part into it
questions.why: Sell a big part into it. A climax run on your own long is a place to sell a big part, and how big is a judgment call. Do not add to it. Do not move the stop to the HVC, which is never the stop.
questions.lesson_line: A burst on your own long is a gift. Sell into it.

wrong.Move the stop to the HVC: The HVC is never the stop. Sell into the burst instead.
wrong.Sell a small part and trail: The rule is a big part. A climax run on your own long is the place to sell into.
wrong.Add more on the next gap: No adding, and a burst is a place to sell.

questions.simple: A burst like this is a climax on your own long, so we sell a big part into it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (C34), a judgment call

questions.q: Flat after day 2. Which one is a follow-up entry of ours at the HVC?
choices: A tight flag over the HVC
A bare touch of the HVC line
A buy at the open on day 3
A buy on a close under the HVC
questions.answer: A tight flag over the HVC
questions.why: A tight flag over the HVC. The follow-up entries are our own setups at the level: an Oops Reversal or an undercut and rally at the HVC, a hold of the 9 or 20 EMA near it, or a tight flag over it. Each has its own trigger and stop.
questions.lesson_line: Later entries at the level are our own setups, each with its own trigger and stop.

wrong.A tight flag over the HVC: That is another of our follow-up setups, with its own trigger and stop.
wrong.A bare touch of the HVC line: A touch alone is not a setup. It has no trigger of its own.
wrong.A buy at the open on day 3: The taught trigger is day 2. A later entry needs one of our own setups, not a buy at the open.
wrong.A buy on a close under the HVC: A close under the HVC is not an entry. A later entry needs one of our own setups at the level.

questions.simple: After day 2 we buy at the level only on one of our own named setups, such as a tight flag over the HVC.

reasons: the follow-up entries are proposed on the card

questions.q: Which stock fits the High Volume Edge card better?
questions.story: Two stocks set lifetime volume records on fresh news, both up big. One traded $14 million a day before. The other traded $3 billion.
choices: The $14 million-a-day name
The $3 billion-a-day name
They fit about the same
Neither; the news decides it
questions.why: The $14 million name. The card wants a lesser-known stock: 50-day dollar volume under about $100 million a day before the event, and not a mega-cap. Bonde also finds that earnings breakouts in widely covered companies do not do as well.
questions.lesson_line: The quieter the name before, the louder the record.

wrong.The $3 billion-a-day name: That is far past the card's line of about $100 million a day. The card rules out the mega-cap.
wrong.They fit about the same: Dollar volume before the day is the test, and these two sit far apart.
wrong.Neither; the news decides it: Both are on fresh news. The size of the name before the day is what separates them.

questions.simple: The $14 million name fits better. The card wants a lesser-known stock and marks down a well-owned one.

reasons: grade cues are proposed on the card

questions.q: Is it an HVE, a PEG or neither?
questions.story: An earnings report sends a stock up 22%. It trades more shares than on any day in its history.
choices: An HVE; the volume is extreme
A PEG; the move came on earnings
Neither; earnings are no catalyst
Neither; a 22% rise is too small
questions.answer: An HVE; the volume is extreme
questions.why: An HVE. Earnings on ordinary big volume is a PEG, but earnings so big the volume is extreme can be an HVE. This stock traded more shares than on any day in its history. DOCU in 2019 was the same case: earnings on all-time record volume, an HVE and not a PEG. Bonde notes that earnings-day volume can be the highest in a stock's history.
questions.lesson_line: Earnings can count. The volume decides, not the report.

wrong.Neither; earnings are no catalyst: Earnings so big the volume is extreme count as a fresh story.
wrong.A PEG; the move came on earnings: A PEG is earnings on ordinary big volume. An all-time record is not ordinary.
wrong.Neither; a 22% rise is too small: The size of the move is not the test here. Record volume on a fresh story is.

questions.simple: An HVE. Earnings can make an HVE when the volume is extreme, a record for the stock's whole history.

reasons: ties to held decision D-089 (record volume vs extreme volume)

questions.q: How does the group read?
questions.story: Four names in one theme all set volume records on the same day. One gives a clean day-2 reclaim of its HVC.
choices: A cue; each still triggers
A rule; all four must trigger
A warning; it is a crowd
A trigger; buy all four
questions.why: A cue. A group or theme setting volume records on the same day is a cue, not a rule. Each name still needs its own day-2 trigger, so only the clean reclaim is a buy.
questions.lesson_line: A group moving together is a tailwind, not a trigger.

wrong.A rule; all four must trigger: The group is a cue, not a rule. Each name needs its own day-2 trigger.
wrong.A warning; it is a crowd: The card reads a group setting records the same day as a help, not a warning.
wrong.A trigger; buy all four: A group is not a trigger. A name with no day-2 reclaim is no trade.

questions.simple: A group setting records the same day helps, but it is only a cue. Each name still needs its own trigger.

reasons: +3 one cited fact only (the card's group cue)
+2 rests on an unsigned UCT note on the card, unmeasured
+1 fixed before (the key was reworded)

questions.q: Account 40,000. Risk 0.5%. Fill 20.18, stop 19.89. Ignore the position cap and round down. How many shares?
questions.why: 689 shares. Risk dollars are 0.5% of 40,000. Divide that by the fill minus the stop, 20.18 minus 19.89, and round down. The size is then the smaller of that and the position cap. If the honest stop does not fit the risk, you skip.
questions.lesson_line: The stop sets the size, never the other way round.
questions.simple: 689 shares. The stop sets the size: divide the dollars you will risk by the distance from fill to stop, then round down.

deeper.example: TVTX, 2015: the HVC was 20.17, so the buy is 20.18 and the stop 19.89. The stop distance is small, so the risk-based share count is large. Work out the stop first, then the size, then check the size against the position cap.

reasons: +2 computed key
+2 rests on the owner's rulebook (A5, the sizing formula and the cap)
+1 fixed before (the fill was corrected)

choices: 689 shares
68 shares
344 shares
9 shares

wrong.68 shares: Slipped the decimal: used a tenth of the risk percent.
wrong.9 shares: Divided the risk dollars by the fill price, not the gap to the stop.

questions.q: A trade under the record day's low ends the level as support, even if the day closes back above it.
questions.why: False. It takes a close under the record day's low to end the level as support. After that close, the HVC is overhead, not a floor. A trade under the low that closes back above it does not end the level. Even a close under the HVC itself is not an invalidation, so do not erase the line.
questions.lesson_line: The level ends on a close under the record day's low.
questions.simple: False, because only a close under the record day's low ends the level as support. A trade under it that closes back does not.

deeper.trap: The trap is treating a poke under the low as the end. The card counts a close. After a close under the low, the HVC is overhead, not a floor: QGEN slid to 38.80, under its 46.07 HVE low, and the level turned into overhead.

reasons: +3 the key rests on one cited fact (the level-ends line)
+2 rests on the card's proposed level rule

questions.q: Where is the stop now?
questions.story: Your High Volume Edge long: buy 50.00, stop 48.50. It gaps open at 47.90, then trades as low as 47.40 in the first 30 minutes.
choices: 47.40, first 30-minute low
Out at the open, 47.90 a share
Back at 48.50, your old stop
46.00, to give it more room
questions.why: 47.40. On a gap through the stop, the low of the first 30-minute bar is the new stop. The loss at that low stays inside the 2R ceiling, so you hold to it. Had it gone past 2R, you would be out.
questions.lesson_line: Let the first 30 minutes set the stop on a gap against you.

wrong.Out at the open, 47.90 a share: The gap rule waits for the first 30 minutes, unless the loss passes 2R.
wrong.Back at 48.50, your old stop: Price already gapped through it. The first 30-minute low sets the new stop.
wrong.46.00, to give it more room: Room is not a rule. The first 30-minute low is the stop.

questions.simple: The first 30-minute low, 47.40, is the new stop, because that loss is still inside the 2R limit.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B20 gap rule)
the key needs a small calculation against the 2R ceiling

questions.q: Gap Support and the High Volume Edge both mark a big up day. Which line does Gap Support defend?
choices: The gap-up day's low
The record day's close
The gap-up day's high
The prior day's close
questions.why: The gap-up day's low. Gap Support defends that low days or weeks later. The High Volume Edge line is the record day's close, the HVC. Find the line first, then you know which setup you are looking at.
questions.lesson_line: Find the line: Gap Support, the gap day's low; HVE, the record day's close.

wrong.The record day's close: That is the HVE's line, the HVC. Gap Support uses the gap day's low.
wrong.The gap-up day's high: The high is not either setup's line.
wrong.The prior day's close: That is where a gap would fill. Gap Support defends the gap-up day's low instead.

questions.simple: Gap Support defends the low of the gap-up day, while the HVE line is the record day's close.

reasons: settled card line, two facts

questions.q: Inside our rules, what would have saved it?
questions.story: You bought day 2 at 331.66, stop 323.98. The next day it reaches 2.3R. Four sessions after the buy, the low trades 322.50 and takes the stop.
choices: Stop to breakeven at 2R
A stop under 320 for room
Selling it all at 2R
Skipping the day-2 trigger
questions.why: Stop to breakeven at 2R. Our rule allows the move anywhere from 2R to 5R. NKTR reached 2.3R, then four sessions after the buy its low of 322.50 took the 323.98 stop. With the stop at breakeven from 2R, that stop-out is a scratch. Left where it was, it is a planned loss.
questions.lesson_line: A 2R gain given back is a scratch once the stop sits at breakeven.

wrong.A stop under 320 for room: Our stop sits a few cents under the day-2 low, and it only moves up, never wider.
wrong.Selling it all at 2R: Selling it all at 2R gives up the run. The first sell is a judgment, usually from day 3 on.
wrong.Skipping the day-2 trigger: The trigger was valid. The breakeven move is the tool.

questions.simple: Moving the stop to breakeven once it hit 2R turns this loss into a scratch.

deeper.trap: Breakeven turns a loss into a scratch, but it can still shake you out before a run. NKTR made 373.20 two days after its stop traded. That is the cost of a tight stop, not a reason to widen it.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19); the card gives two timings for the breakeven move

questions.q: Which is the one thing you never do?
questions.story: The HVC is 13.11. Day 2 opens 12.80, falls well lower, then reclaims 13.11. The honest stop under the day-2 low is wide. At your usual share count it would risk more than your plan allows.
choices: Pull the stop in to fit
Skip and wait for a later setup
Size down from the real stop
Place the stop under that low
questions.answer: Pull the stop in to fit
questions.why: Pull the stop in to fit. The stop comes first, a few cents under the day-2 low. Past 5% away, we mostly skip and wait for a tighter trigger. NAVN's honest day-2 stop was 7.5% wide. Never move the stop up to make a trade fit.
questions.lesson_line: Never move the stop to fit the size. Move the size, or skip.

wrong.Skip and wait for a later setup: That is the usual call when the stop is past 5% away. Skip, then wait for a tighter trigger.
wrong.Size down from the real stop: Sizing from the real stop is honest. Past 5% away, we mostly skip and wait instead.
wrong.Place the stop under that low: Stop first, a few cents under the day-2 low, is the honest stop. The skip or size call comes after.

questions.simple: Never pull the stop in to make the size fit. Keep the honest stop and let the size, or a skip, follow.

deeper.trap: The stop is the exit, and an exit moved to fit the size is not the honest one. NAVN opened at 12.80 under its 13.11 HVC and traded through it. But the day-2 low was 7.2% under the HVC, so the honest stop was 7.5% wide.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A3) and the pending stop-width decision D-005

questions.q: By our rules, what kept this a win?
questions.story: You bought on day 2. 5R comes in two sessions; the peak is day 17. By day 30 it has round-tripped under the HVC.
choices: Part sold into the push, rest trailed
Holding all of it to the very end
A stop sitting right at the HVC
Selling it all on the day-17 peak
questions.answer: Part sold into the push, rest trailed
questions.why: Part sold into the push, and the rest trailed. INOD hit 5R in two sessions, peaked at +47% on day 17, then round-tripped under the HVC by day 30. Selling part into strength banked the move before the slide.
questions.lesson_line: Sell part into strength. The trail decides the rest.

wrong.Holding all of it to the very end: Holding it all rides the round trip back under the HVC.
wrong.A stop sitting right at the HVC: The HVC is never the stop. Selling part into strength did the work.
wrong.Selling it all on the day-17 peak: Nobody can pick the peak in advance, and we sell part and trail the rest. Day 17 only looks like the exit afterwards.

questions.simple: Part sold into strength banked gains before the slide, and the rest was trailed.

deeper.trap: The trap is hindsight: day 17 only looks like the exit afterwards. We do not guess the peak. We sell part into strength on judgment and trail the rest, so the plan banks gains on the way and keeps a share for the run. INOD is the card's clearest picture of why the last part is trailed.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook and the held D-024 (the trail line is not set)
+1 fixed before (the story fill was corrected)

questions.q: Duncan exits on a close under the HVC; our High Volume Edge plan does the same.
questions.why: False. Duncan does add an exit on an end-of-day close below the HVC. We do not. Our exit is the stop, a few cents under the day-2 low. Trading or closing under the HVC is not an invalidation of the level.
questions.lesson_line: Our exit is the stop, not a close under the line.
questions.simple: False. Duncan sells on a close under the HVC, but our exit is the stop under the day-2 low.

deeper.trap: Do not borrow one piece of Duncan's plan. He buys the close of the gap-up day and exits on a close below the HVC. That exit goes with his entry, not ours.

reasons: rests on the card's stop rule; contrasts a web source

questions.q: Does the 50-day rule it out?
questions.story: A beaten-down stock sets a lifetime volume record on fresh news and closes up, still under its 50-day. Day 2 reclaims the HVC above the 200-day.
choices: No; there is no 50-day rule
Yes; it must be over the 50-day
Yes; the 50 must top the 200
No; the 21-day is the test
questions.why: No. The card has no 10, 21 or 50-day requirement on the HVE day. The 200-day is the line, and the trade, not the record day, must be above it at entry. Here the day-2 reclaim is above the 200-day, so the 50-day does not rule it out.
questions.lesson_line: The 200-day decides. The shorter averages do not.

wrong.Yes; it must be over the 50-day: No 50-day test applies on this card. The 200-day at the fill does.
wrong.Yes; the 50 must top the 200: That is a check for other setups. The HVE has no 50-day requirement.
wrong.No; the 21-day is the test: The card has no 10, 21 or 50-day requirement. The 200-day at the fill is the one line.

questions.simple: No, the card has no 10, 21 or 50-day rule on the record day. The 200-day at the fill is the line.

deeper.trap: The trap is importing a rule this card does not have. On the record day it names no 10, 21 or 50-day requirement. It checks the 200-day at the moment of entry, on the trade, not on the record day.

reasons: +2 rests on the card's proposed no-average rule
+1 fixed before (a wrong note was reworded)

questions.q: Does the flat open rule it out?
questions.story: A stock opens flat, then grinds higher all day on fresh news. It closes near the high on the most shares in its history.
choices: No; the gap is a cue, not a rule
Yes; a gap is required to count
Yes; it needs a gap above 3%
No; but buy the opening-range break
questions.answer: No; the gap is a cue, not a rule
questions.why: No. The opening gap is a cue, not a rule. ERAS gapped 3% and FUN only 0.5%, so the card sets no minimum. A flat open is fine if the day has the rest: record volume, an up close and a fresh story. A close in the upper half of the range helps the grade. This stock grinds up and closes near its high on the most shares in its history. The flat open does not rule it out.
questions.lesson_line: Gap or no gap, a record up day can be an HVE.

wrong.Yes; a gap is required to count: The card calls the gap a cue, not a rule.
wrong.Yes; it needs a gap above 3%: ERAS gapped 3% and FUN only 0.5%. Neither number is a minimum.
wrong.No; but buy the opening-range break: An opening-range break is the Episodic Pivot's buy on the gap day itself. The HVE waits a session.

questions.simple: A flat open does not rule it out. The gap is only a cue, so the rest of the card still has to fit.

deeper.counter: Do not turn an example into a threshold. ERAS gapped 3% and FUN 0.5%. Neither number is a minimum, and the card calls the gap a cue, not a rule.

reasons: card cue, with two good examples

questions.q: What does that close say about the day?
questions.story: Up 100% on 62 times its 50-day average volume, 10 times the old record. But it closes at 0.26 of the day's range.
choices: A weak sign; it closed too low
A strong sign; volume is huge
A strong sign; move is huge
A weak sign; it ended down
questions.answer: A weak sign; it closed too low
questions.why: A weak sign. The card wants the close in the upper half of the day's range, 0.7 or more preferred. That is a grade cue, not a hard line. A close in the lower half of a huge range counts against the day. MBX was up 100% on 62x its average volume but closed at 0.26 of its range. Its day-2 reclaim never saw a cent of profit.
questions.lesson_line: A record day should close strong. A low close counts against it.

wrong.A strong sign; volume is huge: Volume is not the whole picture. The close tells who won the day.
wrong.A strong sign; move is huge: The move is big, the close is weak. The card wants the close in the upper half of the range.
wrong.A weak sign; it ended down: It closed up 100% on the day. The weak part is where in the range it closed.

questions.simple: A close low in the day's range is a weak sign, even on huge volume.

deeper.trap: Size does not carry the day, the close does. MBX was up 100% on 62x the 50-day volume and 10x the old record. It still closed at 0.26 of its range, and its day-2 reclaim with a 7.4% stop never saw a cent of profit.

reasons: the close grade is a cue, not a hard line

questions.q: HVE or not?
questions.story: A mega-cap everyone owns trades its biggest volume in a year, with no earnings report. That is about 3 times its average, and it closes up 7%.
choices: Not an HVE; just a big day
An HVE; it is a one-year record
An HVE; it closed up on volume
A PEG; it is a well-owned name
questions.answer: Not an HVE; just a big day
questions.why: Not an HVE. Calling any year-high volume an HVE is a named mistake, and a 3x day on a mega-cap is that mistake. The card wants a lesser-known name with a fresh story, not a mega-cap. Duncan's focus is not any high volume but the highest volume.
questions.lesson_line: A big day in a mega-cap is not an edge.

wrong.An HVE; it is a one-year record: A year-high on a mega-cap is not an HVE.
wrong.An HVE; it closed up on volume: An up close is needed but not enough. The name and the size of the record fail.

questions.q: What happened, by the plan?
questions.story: An earnings record day. You buy day 2 at 48.34, stop 47.52, a real stop order with the broker. Day 3 opens 49.56 and reverses to 46.94.
choices: Stopped; a small planned loss
Still in; it closed over the HVC
A mistake; the stop was too tight
Stopped; the loss broke the plan
questions.why: Stopped, a small planned loss. You bought at 48.34 with the stop at 47.52, 1.7% under the buy, as a real stop order with the broker. Day 3 opened at 49.56 and reversed to 46.94, through the stop, so the order took the trade out. The stop is the exit, and a tight day-2 stop is the design: the first sessions decide the trade.
questions.lesson_line: A real stop order acts when you cannot. That is its job.

wrong.Still in; it closed over the HVC: Yesterday's close does not hold today. The stop traded at 47.52.
wrong.A mistake; the stop was too tight: Tight day-2 stops are the design. The first sessions decide the trade.
wrong.Stopped; the loss broke the plan: The stop is the exit, so a stop-out is the plan working, not a broken plan.

questions.simple: The stop order sold the trade when price fell through it. That is a small planned loss.

deeper.example: YELP, 2018: the day-2 buy at 48.34 had its stop at 47.52, 1.7% under it. The next session opened at 49.56, then fell to 46.94 and took the stop. A tight stop makes a small loss when a day-2 trade fails, and that is the design.

reasons: +2 rests on the owner's rulebook (D41, a real stop order)
+1 fixed before (an unsupported line was removed)

questions.why: False. Duncan's hard stop is 3% to 5% under the HVC. Ours is a few cents under the day-2 low, the low made before the reclaim. It is never the HVC itself.
questions.lesson_line: Our stop comes from the chart: the day-2 low, not a set percent.
questions.simple: False. Duncan uses a set 3% to 5% under the HVC, but our stop sits a few cents under the day-2 low.

deeper.counter: Duncan's stop fits his plan: he buys the close of the gap-up day and sets it 3% to 5% under. Ours buys day 2 and takes its stop from the chart. That stop was 1.0% wide for VRTX and 7.5% wide for NAVN.

questions.q: On a tight day-2 stop, 3R is only a few percent over the buy. That makes 3R a good fixed place to sell a third.
questions.why: False. A tight stop puts 3R only 3% to 7% over the buy, and most winners got there the next session. But the first sell is a judgment, not a fixed third at 3R. We usually wait until day 3 at the earliest.
questions.lesson_line: 3R is a mark, not a sell order. Read the percent, then judge.
questions.simple: False. 3R is only a few percent over the buy, but the first sell is still a judgment call.

deeper.counter: A small percent does not make the target smaller in R. Three times the risk is still 3R, whether the stop is 1.0% or 3.5% wide. Read the percent so you know what the move looks like, then judge the first sell.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B19 first trim)

questions.q: What do you do?
questions.story: The market reading turns Red. A clean High Volume Edge gives its day-2 reclaim.
choices: Mostly cash; pass on it
Buy it, but at full size
Buy it, but at half size
Short it; the market is Red
questions.why: Mostly cash; pass on it. Red means mostly cash and shorts, and a clean HVE is still a long. Green is full risk, Yellow is smaller and fewer, and Orange is only A+ setups. Never force a trade to have something on. Cash is a position.
questions.lesson_line: Red market, mostly cash. The setup can wait.

wrong.Buy it, but at full size: Full risk is a Green market. Red is mostly cash.
wrong.Buy it, but at half size: Smaller and fewer is Yellow. Red is mostly cash and shorts.
wrong.Short it; the market is Red: The HVE is long only. Red does allow shorts, but not a short of this setup.

questions.simple: In a Red market we stay mostly in cash, so we pass even on a clean setup.

deeper.trap: The reading is a guide, not a switch. Green allows full risk per grade and up to 10 positions, Yellow smaller and fewer, Orange only A+ setups. Red is mostly cash and shorts, and the HVE is long only, so a clean one still waits.

reasons: rests on the owner's market reading (F65)

questions.q: Hold through the report?
questions.story: Your High Volume Edge long is up 3.2R. The company reports in two days.
choices: Sell before the report
Sell right after the report
Hold; the level is strong
Hold; stop to breakeven
questions.why: Sell before the report. Hold through a report only if the trade is up 5R, and this one is up 3.2R. The same window bars new buys in the 3 sessions before a report. The level and a breakeven stop do not change the rule.
questions.lesson_line: Into a report, only a 5R cushion stays.

wrong.Sell right after the report: That holds the trade through the report. Under 5R, you sell before it.
wrong.Hold; the level is strong: The level does not change the rule. Under 5R, sell before the report.
wrong.Hold; stop to breakeven: Breakeven comes between 2R and 5R, but the report rule is separate: hold only if up 5R.

questions.simple: Sell before the report. You may hold through it only when the trade is up 5R, and this one is 3.2R.

deeper.trap: The rule has two halves. No new buys in the 3 days before a report, and no holding through one unless the trade is up 5R. The level and a breakeven stop change neither half.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (B22 earnings window)

questions.why: True. Shannon writes that you can fix the anchor from meaningful market events, not just fixed time periods. His example anchors at a large price movement event. Our HVE day is a record-volume up day, so its AVWAP starts there and stays on the chart for months. The card sets our rule, not Shannon.
questions.lesson_line: Anchor the AVWAP where the story changed.
questions.simple: True. Shannon anchors a VWAP at a large price move or other market event, and our record day is one.

questions.q: Write the plan: entry and stop.
questions.story: A quiet stock trades record volume, up 41%, and closes near its high at 32.50. Day 2 dips under that close to a low of 31.80, then trades back through it. You keep two cents of room on a stop.
choices: Wait for 34, stop 31.78
Buy at the close, 32.50, stop 31.78
questions.why: 32.51, stop 31.78. The buy is a market order a cent over the HVC. The stop is two cents under the day-2 low of 31.80, never the HVC. The first sell is a judgment made later.
questions.lesson_line: Entry and stop before the buy. Then let the plan work.

wrong.32.51, stop 32.48: The HVC is never the stop. It sits under the day-2 low, not under the HVC.
wrong.Wait for 34, stop 31.78: The trigger is the trade back over the HVC, not a higher price. 34 would also be past the 4% chase limit.
wrong.Buy at the close, 32.50, stop 31.78: We buy as price trades back over the HVC, never at the close.

questions.simple: Buy a cent over the HVC at 32.51 and put the stop two cents under the day-2 low at 31.78.

deeper.example: The plan is written before the buy: entry 32.51, stop 31.78. The same plan applies on the trade that fails, because the stop is the exit.
